exercises.objective: Apply the STRIPS frame assumption to derive the resulting state after an action.
exercises.prompt: State $s=\{\text{box}(a),\text{box}(b),\text{ball}(c),\text{table}(d),\text{on}(a,b),\text{on}(b,d),\text{on}(c,d),\text{inhand}(\text{nil})\}$. Action $\text{grab}(c)$ has effect $\{\text{inhand}(c),\neg\text{on}(c,d)\}$. State whether $\text{on}(a,b)$ is true in the resulting state $s'$, and explain why, using the frame assumption.
hints: The frame assumption says every fact *not mentioned in the effect* stays unchanged after the action.
$\text{on}(a,b)$ does not appear in $\text{grab}(c)$'s effect $\{\text{inhand}(c),\neg\text{on}(c,d)\}$ at all.
So $\text{on}(a,b)$ is unaffected by the frame assumption and remains true in $s'$, exactly as it was in $s$; only $\text{inhand}$ and $\text{on}(c,d)$ actually change.

exercises.objective: Compute the order of magnitude of a symbolic state space for a modest number of objects.
exercises.prompt: For $n=20$ objects, the state space size is roughly $2^{n^2}$. Compute $\log_{10}(2^{400})$ to confirm the source's claim that this is $\approx10^{120}$. Enter a decimal (round to 1 decimal place).
hints: $400\times0.301\approx120.4$: confirming $2^{400}\approx10^{120.4}$, an astronomically large state space from just 20 objects, far too large to observe densely enough to safely infer deterministic rules. (Independently verified with Python while authoring this module.)

exercises.objective: Compute the probability that a probabilistic relational rule's intended effect fails to occur.
exercises.prompt: For the $\text{grab}(X)$ rule with outcomes $0.7:\text{inhand}(X),\neg\text{on}(X,Y)$; $0.2:\text{on}(X,Z),\neg\text{on}(X,Y)$; $0.1:\text{noise}$, compute the probability that the grab does *not* result in the object being in hand. Enter a decimal.
hints: 'In hand' corresponds only to the first outcome, with probability $0.7$.
The probability of *not* achieving this is the sum of the other two outcomes' probabilities.
$0.2+0.1=0.3$: a 30% chance the grab fails to put the object in hand (it either slides to a new location or produces an unmodeled/noisy outcome).

exercises.objective: Explain why uncertainty in a rule representation makes it learnable, connecting to ML-02's regularization.
exercises.prompt: Explain why a deterministic STRIPS rule is an 'all-or-nothing' target for learning from noisy data, and why a probabilistic relational rule doesn't have this problem, connecting explicitly to ML-02's regularization idea.
hints: A deterministic rule claims a single, fixed outcome always occurs; a single observed exception (noise, an unusual outcome, sensor error) directly contradicts the rule, forcing either a wrong rule or an ever-more-specific, ever-less-general rule carved out to handle every exception separately.

A probabilistic rule instead just assigns exceptions a small, honest outcome probability (like the grab rule's $0.1:\text{noise}$ term), absorbing noisy or rare observations without needing to explain them away individually.

This is structurally the same move as ML-02's regularization: rather than forcing a model to fit every last data point exactly (risking an overly complex, brittle fit), allowing some 'slack' (regularization penalty there, an explicit noise-outcome probability here) trades a small amount of fit for a much more compact, strongly-generalizing rule set, learnable from far less data.
